name: runtime-and-scaling
title: Runtime and scaling: throughput and scaling curves for the Rust engine
question:
After the ~23x performance pass and the addition of configurable PDE
parameters, how does the viva-biofilm engine's wall-time scale with grid
size, agent population, and run duration -- and what throughput
(agent-steps/sec) does it sustain?

report.title: Runtime and scaling
report.evidence_quality: deterministic sweeps (fixed seed per config, no statistical repeats)
report.objective:
Measure wall-time and throughput across three independent scaling axes
(grid resolution, initial population, run duration) at fixed, modest
per-point step counts, and produce interactive scaling curves alongside
a throughput summary.
report.result:
Grid sweep (40 agents, 40 steps): 0.198 ms/step at 512 cells (16x32) to
3.189 ms/step at 12288 cells (96x128) -- sub-linear-to-linear growth in
cells, no configuration slow (<30s threshold). Population sweep (grid
48x64, 40 steps): 0.219 ms/step at 20 final agents to 2.387 ms/step at
320 final agents. Duration sweep (grid 48x64, 40 agents): total wall time
0.014s at 20 steps to 0.669s at 160 steps; a linear fit of total time vs.
steps gives R^2=0.907 -- close to linear but not exact, because
population grows via division over the course of a run (40 -> 640
agents over 160 steps), which compounds per-step cost as the run
lengthens. Absolute throughput is single-threaded and machine-load-
dependent: the per-step timings above and a peak of ~3e5 agent-steps/sec
were measured on an unloaded machine, while the same sweeps re-run under
heavy concurrent load recorded ~1.4e4 agent-steps/sec. The robust,
hardware-independent result is the SCALING SHAPE above, not the absolute
rate; a clean re-run on an idle machine is needed for a representative
peak figure.
report.interpretation:
The engine is fast and its scaling is well-behaved: no configuration in
any of the three fixed sweeps approached the 30s slow threshold (worst
case 0.13s for the largest grid, 0.67s for the longest duration run).
Grid and population scaling both show a clear, roughly proportional cost
increase with problem size. Duration scaling is "near-linear" rather
than exactly linear -- the R^2=0.907 fit reflects a genuine effect (later
steps cost more because the population has grown), not measurement
noise, and is reported here rather than smoothed over.

study_card.one_liner: Single-threaded throughput ~1.4e4-3e5 agent-steps/sec (machine-load-dependent); grid/population/duration scaling curves all produced, no slow configs.
study_card.headline: PASS — fast, well-scaling, throughput measured.
